items.title: The Twelve Marks of a Mind That Has Released Desire (Part 1)

items.zh: 云何於諸欲中心不趣入？謂於彼處不見勝功德故。云何不美？謂於彼處喜悅不生故。云何不住？謂於彼處不樂受用為欣悅故。
items.en: What is it for the mind not to enter into desires? It is that one sees in them no superior merit. What is "finding no charm"? It is that no delight arises there. What is "not settling in"? It is that one takes no pleasure in their enjoyment, finding in it nothing to be glad about.

items.zh: 云何無有勝解？謂於彼處不樂取著不如理相故。云何萎顇？謂雖縱任而不舒泰故。云何壞散？謂取境已，尋復棄捨故。
items.en: What is "having no fascination"? It is that one takes no pleasure in grasping their unwarranted marks. What is "withering"? It is that even when the mind is given free rein, it finds no ease. What is "letting fall"? It is that, having taken up the object, one at once discards it again.

items.title: The Twelve Marks of a Mind That Has Released Desire (Part 2): Equanimity and Revulsion

items.zh: 云何而不舒泰？謂於所緣雖強令住，而不愛樂故。云何等住於捨？謂行平等位，於平等位中心遊觀故。
items.en: What is "still finding no ease"? It is that, although one forcibly makes the mind dwell upon the object, it takes no fond pleasure in it. What is "resting evenly in equanimity"? It is that one proceeds in a state of evenness, the mind roving and observing within that even state.

items.zh: 何等為厭？謂由於彼深見過患，棄背為性。此復三種。謂無常故、苦故、變壞法故。何等為惡？謂由於彼初見過患，棄背為性。何等為違？謂由於彼中見過患，棄背為性。何等為背？謂由於彼後見過患，棄背為性。
items.en: What is revulsion? By seeing deeply the faults in them, its very nature is to abandon and turn away. This is again threefold: because they are impermanent, because they are suffering, because they are subject to decay. What is "aversion"? By seeing the fault in them at the outset, its nature is to abandon and turn away. What is "opposition"? By seeing the fault in the midst of them, its nature is to abandon and turn away. What is "turning the back"? By seeing the fault in them at the last, its nature is to abandon and turn away.

items.title: The Mirror Image: Four Marks of a Mind Entering the Release from Desire

items.zh: 與此相違，即於離欲作意趣入者，謂於是處見勝功德故。美者，謂於是處生清淨信而證順故。住者，謂於所緣不流散故。
items.en: Contrary to all the above, "the attention that enters into the release from desire" means that here one does see superior merit. "Charm" means that here a pure faith arises and one accords with its realisation. "Settling" means that the mind does not scatter away from its object.

items.zh: 勝解者，由於是處不染污轉，於諸煩惱得離繫故。以於厭等棄背行中正流轉時，心無罣礙。又復於捨無有功用。
items.en: "Firm conviction" means that here the mind proceeds undefiled and so becomes unbound from the afflictions — because when it flows on within the practice of revulsion and turning-away, the mind meets no obstruction; and moreover, it lets the object fall with no effort at all.

items.title: "The Mind Well Gone": The Vajra-Like Concentration and the Attentions That Lead to It

items.zh: 云何其心善逝？謂住方便究竟作意故。云何善修？謂善修習餘作意故。當知此說斷位及斷方便道位。
items.en: What is "the mind well gone"? It is abiding in the attention of the consummation of means. What is "well cultivated"? It is thoroughly cultivating the remaining attentions. Know that this speaks of the position of actual severance and the position of the preparatory path to severance.

items.title: Three Words for Freedom: Loosed from Entanglements, Released from the Object, Unbound from the Seed

items.zh: 解者，謂解脫諸纏故。脫者，謂解脫所緣相故。離繫者，謂解脫隨眠故。
items.en: "Loosed" means freed from the active entanglements. "Released" means freed from the object-mark. "Unbound" means freed from the latent tendency.

items.title: Four Faults of Desire, and Being Freed, Transcending, and Unbound from Them

items.zh: 從諸欲緣所生諸漏者，謂除欲貪，於欲界中所餘煩惱。損匱者，謂因此生執器仗等惡行差別，於此若作、若增長故，生諸惡趣。燒者：謂由此因、欲愛噉食、燒身心故。惱者，謂由此因，若事變壞，便生愁歎憂苦惱故。
items.en: "The outflows born with desire as their condition" means, apart from craving for desire itself, all the remaining afflictions of the desire realm. "Ruinous loss" means that from this arise the various evil deeds of taking up weapons and the like; by committing and repeating them, one is born into the evil destinies. "Burning" means that through this cause, the craving of desire devours one, scorching body and mind. "Distress" means that through this cause, when the desired thing decays, there arise sorrow, lament, anxiety, pain, and affliction.

items.zh: 於彼解脫、超出、離繫者，謂如前次第，解脫諸纏、所緣、隨眠故。
items.en: As for being freed from, transcending, and unbound from them: this is, in the prior sequence, being loosed from the entanglements, released from the object, and unbound from the latent tendency.

items.title: Why the Sage Never "Receives" the Feelings Desire Conditions — the Red Lotus and the Water-Drop

items.zh: 云何終不領納緣彼諸受？謂依將得、正得、隨念諸欲境界，染污諸受不復現行；其所依身不為眾惑染污而住，如紅蓮花，水滴不著。
items.en: Why does the sage in the end never take up the feelings conditioned by those desires? Because, whether in relation to desire-objects about to be gained, presently being gained, or merely called to mind, the defiled feelings no longer manifest; the body that supports him abides unstained by the host of afflictions — like a red lotus, to which a water-drop does not cling.

items.title: The Six Gateways of Favourable Release — and the Practitioner Still Pierced by the Poison-Arrow of Doubt

items.zh: 復有六種順出離界，如經廣說。謂我已修慈，乃至我已離諸我慢，然我猶為疑惑毒箭悶亂其心。是故慈等於恚、害等非正對治。
items.en: There are furthermore six gateways of favourable release, as the scriptures explain at length. … [Someone objects:] "I have cultivated loving-kindness, and so on up to: I have abandoned all conceits of self; yet the poison-arrow of doubt still bewilders my mind — therefore loving-kindness and the rest are not the true antidote for ill-will, harm, and the like."

items.title: Answering the Objection: Why Each of the Six Gateways Is Established

items.zh: 當知為捨如是邪執，建立此界。是中恚等離欲對治有差別故，建立前四。對治相故，觀察聖住得道理故，建立無相。觀察究竟正道理故，建立第六。
items.en: Know that it is in order to abandon such wrong grasping that this set of gateways is established. Herein, because the antidotes by which one becomes free of ill-will and the rest differ, the first four are established. Because it counters [grasping at] marks, and because through it one investigates and attains the principle of the noble abidings, the signless is established. Because it investigates the ultimate correct principle [of one's own realisation], the sixth is established.

items.title: The Six Antidotes Explained (Part 1): Loving-Kindness, Compassion, and Sympathetic Joy

items.zh: 慈對治恚，無損行轉故。悲對治害，為除他苦，勝樂行轉故。喜治不樂，於他樂事隨喜行轉故。
items.en: Loving-kindness counters ill-will, for it proceeds as conduct that does no injury. Compassion counters the wish to harm, for, in order to remove others' suffering, it proceeds as conduct of surpassing joy. Sympathetic joy counters displeasure, for it proceeds as rejoicing in others' happy circumstances.

items.title: The Six Antidotes Explained (Part 2): Equanimity, the Signless, Abandoning Self-Conceit — and Why Poor Practice Lets the Faults Return

items.zh: 捨治貪恚，俱捨行轉故。無相對治一切眾相，相相違故。若離我慢，於自解脫或所證中定無疑惑。故離我慢是彼對治。
items.en: Equanimity counters both craving and ill-will, for it proceeds as conduct that is neither glad nor grieved. The signless counters all the manifold marks, for it is contrary to marks. If one abandons the conceit of self, then regarding one's own liberation or what one has realised there is definitely no doubt; therefore abandoning the conceit of self is the antidote to [that doubt].

items.zh: 此諸出離定能出離一切恚等。不善修故，恚等過失容可現行。
items.en: These releases are certainly able to release one from all ill-will and the rest. It is only through failing to cultivate them well that the faults of ill-will and the rest may still manifest.

items.title: Where the Gateways Belong: Heavenly Abidings, Noble Abidings, and Brahmā-Abidings

items.zh: 又前五種順出離界，初之四種天住所攝，第五一種聖住所攝。今此六種順出離界，前之四種梵住所攝，第五、第六、聖住所攝。
items.en: Furthermore, of the former five gateways of favourable release, the first four are subsumed under the heavenly abidings, and the fifth alone under the noble abidings. Of the present six gateways of favourable release, the first four are subsumed under the Brahmā-abidings, and the fifth and sixth under the noble abidings.

items.title: What Release Rests On: The Four Reliances

items.zh: 復次，能超恚等諸過失故，名為出離。於出離時正可憑仗，故名為依。世尊說依略有四種。一、法是依，非數取趣；二、義是依，非文；三、了義經是依，非不了義經；四、智是依，非識。
items.en: Furthermore, because it can transcend the faults of ill-will and the rest, it is called "release"; because at the time of release it is precisely what one can rely upon, it is called a "reliance." The World-Honoured One taught that reliances are, in brief, of four kinds: first, the Dharma is the reliance, not the person; second, the meaning is the reliance, not the letter; third, the sūtras of definitive meaning are the reliance, not those of provisional meaning; fourth, wisdom is the reliance, not [ordinary] consciousness.

blocks.text: Today's reading describes what a mind free of desire is like, in twelve marks, and then gives six more gateways of release with their antidotes, including the four immeasurables. It ends by introducing the **four reliances**, one of the most quoted teachings in Mahāyāna Buddhism.

subs.head: Twelve marks of a mind free of desire

blocks.text: The mind "does not enter into desires": it "sees in them no superior merit". It finds no charm in them, does not dwell on them, rests evenly in equanimity towards them, and turns away. Master Cháng Bǎi distinguishes this equanimity from mere neutrality: "through wise observation one changes the defiled mind into purity". Venerable Miào Jìng reads the three words for revulsion (aversion, opposition, turning away) as three stages of seeing desire's faults: first, further, and final.
One entering this state "lets the object fall with no effort". Master Cháng Bǎi: "when desire appears one lets go at once, without deliberate attention." What begins as effort becomes spontaneous.
The mind that has arrived is called "**well gone**" (善逝), an epithet of the Buddha, used here, Master Cháng Bǎi says, to praise an arhat's complete freedom from desire.

Three words for freedom: **loosed** from the active entanglements, **released** from the object's mark, **unbound** from the latent tendency. Master Cháng Bǎi: "loosed" is said of the knowing mind; "released", of the object; "unbound", of the seed. The three together cover the moment, the object, and the root.

Desire's faults include "burning". Venerable Miào Jìng: "the craving of desire is a fire, always burning body and mind." The sage "never takes up" the feelings desire conditions, "like a red lotus to which no water-drop clings". Master Cháng Bǎi: the sage's feeling arises from contact joined with insight; ours, from contact joined with ignorance. The feeling itself may be similar; what is joined to it differs.

Six further gateways of release, each with an antidote: **loving-kindness** against ill will, **compassion** against harm, **sympathetic joy** against displeasure (Venerable Miào Jìng: "when I envy you"), **equanimity** against craving and ill will together (Master Cháng Bǎi: "an even mind towards all beings, not closer to some or resentful of others"), the **signless** against the pursuit of signs, and **abandoning self-conceit** against doubt (Venerable Miào Jìng: the subtle conceit of the seventh consciousness).
Someone claims to have cultivated these yet still suffers. The treatise answers: "It is only through failing to cultivate them well" that faults remain. The methods work; poor practice does not.

The first four of the six gateways are the **Brahmā-abidings** (梵住), the four immeasurables; Master Cháng Bǎi: 梵 means "pure", purity through freedom from desire, shared by ordinary and noble beings. Others are **heavenly abidings** (the dhyānas) and **noble abidings** (the gateways of liberation).

Release rests on **four reliances** (四依): rely on the Dharma, not the person; on the meaning, not the letter; on sūtras of definitive meaning, not provisional meaning; on wisdom, not consciousness. Tomorrow's reading explains each against a kind of person.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what does it mean for the mind "not to enter into desires"?
options: seeing in them no superior merit
quiz.why: "What is it for the mind not to enter into desires? It is that one sees in them no superior merit. What is finding no charm? … no delight arises there." Master Cháng Bǎi: like passing through a hundred flowers without a leaf clinging.

quiz.q: What kind of equanimity is "resting evenly in equanimity," and how does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish wholesome from neutral equanimity?
options: wholesome equanimity transforms the defiled mind through wise observation — the power of insight; neutral equanimity just shifts the object, aligned with neither good nor bad
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Through wise observation one changes the defiled mind into purity, aligned with good — this is wholesome equanimity, produced by strong insight." Neutral equanimity just shifts the object. Venerable Miào Jìng: ordinary people have neutral equanimity too.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do "loosed," "released," and "unbound" each refer to?
options: freed from active entanglements, from the object-mark, and from the latent tendency
quiz.why: Loosed means freed from the active entanglements; released, from the object-mark; unbound, from the latent tendency. Master Cháng Bǎi: entanglements are afflictions repeatedly manifesting; unbound means their seeds are cut.

quiz.q: The sage "never takes up" desire-conditioned feelings, like a red lotus shedding water. How do the teachers distinguish the sage's feeling from ours?
options: the sage's feeling arises from contact joined with insight; ours from contact joined with ignorance
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "A sage's feeling arises from contact joined with insight; an ordinary being's from contact joined with ignorance." Venerable Miào Jìng: the sage's senses are joined with prajñā. The text: "the body that supports him abides unstained … like a red lotus, to which a water-drop does not cling."

quiz.q: Someone claims to have cultivated loving-kindness and the rest yet still suffers doubt. Why, per the treatise, can the faults still manifest?
options: through poor cultivation — these releases certainly free one, but practised badly the faults can still appear
quiz.why: "These releases are certainly able to release one from all ill-will and the rest. It is only through failing to cultivate them well that the faults of ill-will and the rest may still manifest." The gateways are established to abandon such wrong grasping. Venerable Miào Jìng: practised fully, they surely work.

quiz.q: The text says sympathetic joy counters "displeasure." What is that displeasure, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: not rejoicing when others succeed in practice — envy
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "When others succeed in practice and I rejoice, that's sympathetic joy; when I don't — when I envy you — that's displeasure." The text: sympathetic joy "proceeds as rejoicing in others' happy circumstances."

quiz.q: The four immeasurables are Brahmā-abidings. What does 梵 mean, and are they shared by ordinary and noble, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: 梵 means pure — purity through freedom from desire; the immeasurables belong to both ordinary and noble
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The four immeasurables belong to the Brahmā-abidings, shared by ordinary and noble. 梵 means purity — purity through freedom from desire." Venerable Miào Jìng: mastering them yields the intermediate dhyāna, even becoming Brahmā king.
